title: Count through hexadecimal glyphs on Digital Lab
audience: Students with basic programming knowledge who are new to assembly
learningObjectives: Distinguish an index, character code, and segment mask
Use a fixed memory-mapped byte port
Verify an ordered I/O protocol and protected-data history
Observe a stable device state in Debug without assuming a repaint per instruction

quiz.prompt: What must the program send to show zero with this wiring?

choices.text: The mask 0x3f.
The integer 0 because the device decodes decimal numbers.
The ASCII byte for the character 0.

hints.text: Decode each set bit using the segment-position table before deciding which numeral it resembles.
Blank is 00, zero is 3f, and one is 06. These are hexadecimal bit patterns, not character codes.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

steps.title: Connect the model and locate its port

quiz.prompt: Does .eqv `RIGHT_DISPLAY` allocate a byte for the display?

choices.text: Yes; it creates the peripheral in ordinary data memory.
Yes; it also writes the first glyph.
No; it names a constant used during assembly.

hints.text: Distinguish the source-header comment, an assembler constant, and a data allocation; only the last reserves data bytes.
Digital Lab Sim should be connected for this execution. Its right port is 0xffff0010; its neighboring control ports are not part of this counter.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

quiz.prompt: Which part of the program changes the device?

choices.text: The label `RIGHT_DISPLAY` executes as a store.
The later store to its port, not this constant load.
Every load into `$s0` changes the device automatically.

hints.text: Loading an address changes a CPU register. Look for a later instruction whose destination is memory.
`$s0` is 0x00000000ffff0010. The device has received no program store.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

steps.title: Locate the table and input words

quiz.prompt: Which address should remain constant while counting?

choices.text: The right-display port address.
The pointer to the current table byte.
The conceptual current digit index.

hints.text: Trace what each address identifies: the device register, the first table byte, or the first input word.
`$s1` identifies table byte zero and `$t0` identifies the first input word. The device pointer remains fixed.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

choices.text: Emit only the entry whose index is sixteen.
Wait sixteen seconds between stores.
Emit sixteen table entries.

hints.text: Each input occupies four bytes. Compute the offset of the count from the address of the starting index.
For the default fixture, the index is zero and the remaining count is sixteen. All valid inputs are small nonnegative values.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

quiz.prompt: Why is no scale-by-four operation needed?

choices.text: The display uses four-byte glyph codes.
Each table element occupies one byte.
All addresses ignore object sizes.

hints.text: Determine the size of one table element before deciding whether the index needs scaling.
For a window starting at fourteen, the cursor is fourteen bytes beyond glyphs. For the empty end window it can equal the one-past-table address without being dereferenced.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

steps.title: Handle an empty window before the loop

quiz.prompt: Why test the count before the first store?

choices.text: An empty window must produce no I/O writes.
Every branch must always be taken.
A zero count names the first display port.

hints.text: Follow the path for a zero count, including the instruction in the branch delay slot.
The empty window exits before the table load and port store. A nonempty window continues to the loop body.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

choices.text: The address of the right display.
An automatically generated ASCII digit.
The selected mask byte, not the index itself.

hints.text: Compare the pointer before the load with the value placed in the destination register afterward.
For default index zero, `$t1` contains 0x3f. The table cursor is an address; the loaded value is the segment mask.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

steps.title: Write one byte to the port

choices.text: The display reads only an instruction mnemonic, not memory.
Adjacent addresses control other parts of the peripheral.
A byte store is merely a faster spelling of every word store.

hints.text: Count the byte addresses covered by a word store starting at the right-display port.
The first program transaction is a byte write of 3f at 0xffff0010. At `displayed`, index and remaining count have not yet been updated.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

quiz.prompt: What would advancing the device pointer by one do?

choices.text: Select a different byte port on the next store.
Select the next digit on the same right display automatically.
Advance the table pointer as well.

hints.text: Ask which object changes its element on the next iteration and which device register receives every output.
The cursor moves to the next table entry. `$s0` still identifies the right port; it must not move to the left or control ports.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

steps.title: Update the logical index and remaining count

quiz.prompt: Which observation boundary has remaining count fifteen after the first output?

choices.text: `displayed`, before the updates.
The initial state before any table load.
`iteration_done`, after the updates.

hints.text: Separate the boundary immediately after the store from the boundary after all three loop-state updates.
After the first default transaction, the next index is one and the remaining count is fifteen. Immediately after the store but before these updates, they were zero and sixteen.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

quiz.prompt: What should be written after the final requested glyph?

choices.text: The first byte beyond the table.
Nothing; the program should exit normally.
A blank mask in every case.

hints.text: Evaluate the branch after the remaining count reaches zero; include its delay-slot instruction.
The default sequence has sixteen byte transactions and ends with mask 71. It does not include a seventeenth write or an automatic blanking write.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

steps.title: Observe a single transaction in Debug

quiz.prompt: Does a completed Run showing F prove that the intermediate glyphs were written?

choices.text: No; the store sequence needs separate evidence.
Yes; the final glyph encodes the entire history.
Yes; the UI always repaints after every instruction.

hints.text: A visible final mask has no record of earlier masks. Decide which observation can establish their order.
After the first store the right mask is 3f. At the eleventh `displayed` hit it is 77 for A. At done it is 71 for F, and the left unit remains blank.

steps.title: Test a short and an empty range

quiz.prompt: What is the expected output sequence for the empty end window?

choices.text: The guard byte after the table.
A blanking write followed by F.
An empty sequence.

hints.text: Write the selected indices as a half-open interval and list its members before simulating the loop.
The short range emits 79, then 71. The empty range emits no port writes. Neither case changes its inputs or table.

completion.reason: Author checks verify the program protocol; native trainer automation is pending.

choices.text: The number of loop iterations.
The decimal point on that display.
The address of the left display.

hints.text: OR the A mask with the decimal-point bit; then express the resulting eight bits as a signed byte initializer.
The A bars remain and the decimal point is added. The bus value is the unsigned byte 247, regardless of the signed initializer used to store its bits.

quiz.prompt: Which property can differ in an equivalent solution?

choices.text: Its register allocation and loop implementation.
The number or order of required device writes.
Which adjacent ports it changes.

hints.text: Derive the exclusive end address from the starting cursor and the requested number of bytes.
Different registers and branch arrangements are accepted when they produce the same byte transactions and preserve the data objects.

steps.title: Verify the protocol and explain the bounds

quiz.prompt: Why is a RAM log written by the student program insufficient by itself?

choices.text: RAM cannot hold byte values.
Every data store automatically drives the right display.
It can describe intended output without proving which device transactions occurred.

hints.text: Consider a program that writes only the last glyph, or changes and restores an input; what evidence would expose each?
The required sequence, port, width, and protected-data behavior must all agree. UI rendering and repaint readiness remain separate integration and capture checks.
